items.title: Harold E. Peterson Interview, 1979-08-06
items.q: that's the guy I first sent John in there, played with George E. Lewis, the banjo player.

ctx.x: Oh, not the one that used to go on up about reeds.

Oh, no, that was John Casimir. Funny thing talking about John Casimir. You know John Casimir. Sure. John Casimir used to use plastic reeds, see. And no matter, any reed I ever got, I used to have to have, I had a special reed, not a special reed, but a reed cutter just for him, for his reeds, see. I used to have to always cut, he'd say to me, they won't play unless you cut part of that reed off for me. Come on, John Casimir. And he called up my wife and said, well, you know, she'd call him and tell him when I got…
And Billy Huntington was another pupil of his.

items.title: Harold E. Peterson Interview, 1979-08-06
items.q: Another, another old, old-time musician used to visit me quite a bit was Red Island's daddy. He used to live over the river, you know, and he used to, once or never, a couple of months, he'd come over and spend about an hour just talking about music

ctx.x: And after the Jazz Band, the original Dixieland Jazz Band made these recordings, then he eliminated the test, see, and anybody could come in then, you see. No, the musicians union in them days, those fellas were all artists, you know. It was a different breed, different breed of musicians, and a happy-go-lucky type, you know. And they were serious musicians, very serious. And like the other guys, you know, they were all, they had a lot of bands that played good, you know, of course, talk about, well, Jules played…
Louie Armstrong and all these different musicians, but did you ever play the banjo? I know you used to sell banjo mutes. They talk about that. Yeah. You kept all different kind of accessories, huh?
